title: Rolling
description: A green-bladed SANYO senpuki in a dim tatami room, seen through a phone camera's rolling shutter. The sensor reads its rows top to bottom over a thirtieth of a second, so every row catches the blades at a later moment than the row above it, and catches the room's fluorescent lamp, which pulses at 120 Hz off the same mains as the motor, at a different point in its flicker: four bands of cool light and warm shade lie across the frame, deep enough to blow out a row of the guard's chrome and drop the row beside it almost to silhouette, the readout made visible. Left alone the fan runs just under 3600 rpm, nearly two turns per readout, so its blades are torn into curling hooks and pieces that float free of the hub, and the whole torn pattern stands almost still against the 30 fps frame rate, creeping slowly backwards while the bands creep up. Drag up to overdrive it; drag down and it coasts through softer hooks and the wagon-wheel speeds. Let go and it returns to speed while the guard in front stays perfectly sharp. Drag sideways to turn the phone, which turns the direction the sensor reads in, and the bands turn with it.
intent: The CMOS rolling shutter (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_shutter), the process behind every phone video of a propeller or a fan, after herb's generative reference 2 (a real photo pulled apart by a real process while the rest of the picture stays intact). The process is a real rolling-shutter capture. A simulated sensor runs at 29.97 fps with a 1/30 s readout and a 1/4000 s exposure per row. Row s of the frame that starts at t0 is exposed over [t0 + s * readout, + exposure] and integrated in linear light over sixteen sub-samples, so the tip smear (about 45 device px at 3590 rpm) is a ramp, not a stack of copies. The room is lit by a ring fluorescent on the same 60 Hz mains as the motor: on an old choke ballast its arc goes out every half cycle while the mains voltage is below 0.55 of its peak and re-strikes after, so its light is a 120 Hz train of broad, flat crests and short dark gaps (the arc's light, saturating with current, as the 0.35 power of the voltage above re-strike). Each phosphor holds it for its own decay time (red 1.6 ms, green 1.1 ms, blue 0.4 ms, a first-order lag applied to each of ten harmonics, plus 3 to 6% of steady light per channel), so blue drops nearly to nothing in the gap while red holds on: the crests run cool at about 1.7 times the mean light and the gaps warm at about a sixth of it, the depth real phone footage under mains tubes shows. Every row integrates the lamp over its own exposure window (each sub-sample lit at its own instant; the plate and guard by its exact mean over the window), so the 1/30 s readout spans exactly four lamp cycles and the frame carries four bright and dark bands along the sensor's rows. They are the readout itself in the picture's own light, not an overlay: they light the plate, the acrylic and the guard through the same linear composite, they turn when the readout direction turns, they shift and wash out as the exposure lengthens (?exp=N for 1/N s; at 1/120 s they vanish, and the blades blur long before that), and since 120 Hz gains 0.004 of a cycle on every 1/29.97 s frame they creep slowly up the frame, about one band every eight seconds, while the torn blades creep backwards. For each sub-sample the rotor is drawn at its angle at that exact instant, read from the rotor's own simulated history at 1/960 s steps, so a fan that speeds up or slows down during a readout shows it at the bottom of the frame. There is no warp. The curls, the floating segments and the wagon-wheel stillness (3 blades x rpm/60 = a multiple of 29.97 Hz, so 599.4, 1198.8 ... 3596.4 rpm) all come from when each row looked. The fan is an induction motor with a set speed (it can push but never brake), quadratic air drag and viscous and dry bearing friction. Left alone it runs as a two-pole motor straight off 60 Hz mains, at 3590 rpm, just under its 3600 rpm synchronous speed (faster than any notch the real fan has, which is what it takes: below about one turn per readout the blades only bend). That is almost two turns per readout, so every blade is read several times down the frame, as hooks and as islands torn off it, and the blades pass at just under 6 x 29.97 Hz, so the torn pattern holds and creeps backwards. Drag or scroll up to overdrive it (to 5400 rpm, thinner and more numerous islands), drag down to drop the set speed so the rotor coasts down on its own drag through the hooks and the wagon-wheel speeds, and let go to return it to mains speed. Drag sideways to rotate the sensor's readout direction. The fan head is turned, so the rotor turns in its own tilted plane: an ellipse fitted to the guard rim maps the picture to the disc and back, about a centre on the rim-to-badge axis where the three blade tips reach the same radius (within 1%). The photo is the 3840 px rendition resampled to 2560 px, and the print is cut tight to the fan head, so the guard and blades fill the frame; it is drawn at no more than one photo pixel per device pixel, so the wires stay crisp at DPR 2. It is cut in three by tools/depth/bakes/rolling/bake.py. The plate is the back of the guard and the motor, and the room behind is pulled down to a dim, nearly grey ground (everything that is not steel, keyed by a lightness top-hat and neutrality), the room lit only by the ceiling lamp. The rotor is the three blades as transmissive acrylic. The readout shears every row of a turning blade by a different angle, so any burr on its outline is drawn out into a frayed stroke end and any fine texture inside it into striations along the rows. So each blade's outline is refitted in the disc's own plane as a low-order Fourier curve (the greenness edge with the notches the wires and the badge's shadow bit out of it closed, then low-passed along its length), one smooth edge with one continuous tip arc, stored as a signed distance field, so every curl and floating segment is a crisp moulded piece, anti-aliased over 0.6 device px. Its look is a field in blade coordinates (radius and chord) that is smooth along every row: the photo's hub-to-tip and chordwise light fitted as a low-order polynomial over the three blades, their one mean green, two crisp broad gloss bands (a long highlight near the leading edge and one across the blade at mid radius), and a moulded lip a few px wide that is denser and a deeper green, so each piece is framed like glass. The engine draws a bright edge a device px inside the outline, lit by the ceiling lamp as far as the outline's normal (the distance field's gradient, carried through each sub-sample's turn) faces it, so the glint runs round each torn piece as it turns. Each exposure sub-sample composites plate x T + E in linear light, with T = 1 - c + c (1 - A) tint and E = c (A body + gloss) + edge. Inside the disc the rotor sweeps, the plate keeps nothing of the photo (tools/depth/bakes/rolling/reveal.py), so no still, blade-shaped shadow of the photographed blades is left under the torn ones: the dim room continues through, the rear guard is drawn over it (its radial spokes and concentric rings as anti-aliased lines in the rim ellipse's tilted plane, about the point the photo's own spokes converge on, darker than the front and a little out of focus), and the motor housing sits behind the hub, lit from the ceiling lamp. The front guard's wires are cut from the photo itself (tools/depth/bakes/rolling/photo_front.py): a ridge filter steered along their own direction says where a front wire runs (the rear guard's crossing wires and the blades' edges run well off it), and the photo's luminance against the ground beside the wire gives its matte, so each wire is as wide as the photo shows it, keeps the steel's own shading and highlights (unmixed from the green or blue its soft edge caught), crosses over a blade wherever it turns, and runs on out to the rim, where it fades into the same photographed wires the plate keeps instead of ending in mid-air. The spoke count (107), phase, width and colour are measured from the photo's rear-guard steel round the blades, so every gap and every floating fragment shows crisp tinted wires behind clean acrylic. The acrylic owns only its colour, its gloss and its edge; the paper sticker on one blade root is taken out. The front is the steel guard wires and the chrome badge. Over the paper sticker on one blade root the wires are patched from round it. The sheet is 0.42 opaque (0.8 at the lip), so the dim room and the rear guard show through it, tinted green. The badge's slots (an annulus fitted between its rings, everything but the chrome spokes) stay open onto the turning blade roots and the motor behind them. The hero is ?rpm=3590&t=0.4, the speed the fan runs at on its own: the blades torn into hooks round the hub and two islands floating free at the top. ?rpm=4800&t=0.25 holds the frame (t a multiple of 1/120 s starts the frame at the lamp's trough) that starts at t seconds with the rotor at a steady rpm; ?rpm=1420&t=0.25 is the old desk-fan speed, where the blades only bend. ?scan=degrees sets the readout direction.
sources: Photo: "EF-C30N electric fan which we can understand when SANYO Electrics manufactured (2)" by Tokumeigakarinoaoshima, Wikimedia Commons, CC0 1.0 (public domain dedication). https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:EF-C30N_electric_fan_which_we_can_understand_when_SANYO_Electrics_manufactured_(2).jpg (3840 px rendition, resampled to 2560 px). A SANYO EF-C30N senpuki (logo in use 1976-1986), photographed 2013-06-16. Cropped tight to the fan head, the room behind it graded down to a dim ground, and cut into plate, rotor and front by tools/depth/bakes/rolling/bake.py, with the rear guard behind the blades drawn by tools/depth/bakes/rolling/reveal.py.
